title: Saducismus Triumphatus, or Full and Plain Evidence Concerning Witches and Apparitions
author: Joseph Glanvill (posthumous, ed. Henry More)
publisher: London (posthumous first full edition; precursor versions from 1666)
subject_focus: Systematic empirical defense of witch-belief and the reality of spirits against Hobbesian materialism, combining philosophical argument with case studies compiled on Baconian natural-history principles; edited posthumously by Henry More with additional philosophical apparatus.
summary: Joseph Glanvill's Saducismus Triumphatus (1681) is the most intellectually ambitious defense of witch-belief produced in Restoration England and the work most important for Clark's argument that the Scientific Revolution did not cause the decline of witch prosecution. The title announces its program: 'Sadducism' (Glanvill's term for Hobbesian materialism, after the biblical sect that denied resurrection) has been overcome (triumphatus). The work's first part develops the philosophical argument that rejecting spirit-phenomena is not scientific scepticism but materialist dogmatism, since the Royal Society's empirical methodology requires taking reliable testimony to preternatural phenomena as seriously as any other class of evidence. The second part collects case studies — including Glanvill's own investigation of the Drummer of Tedworth (1662) — documented in Baconian natural-history style. Henry More edited and expanded the posthumous 1681 edition with additional philosophical apparatus connecting Glanvill's empirical case to the Cambridge Platonist anti-Hobbes program. The work went through multiple subsequent editions and was widely read in England and New England, where its influence on Cotton Mather and the Salem proceedings has been debated.
scholarly_significance: Saducismus Triumphatus is the primary source for Clark's extended analysis of 'scientific demonology' in Restoration England (Thinking with Demons, Part II: Science, pp.356–375). Clark uses it to demonstrate three connected points: (1) that the most scientifically sophisticated figures of the Restoration period — Fellows of the Royal Society — were simultaneously the most systematic defenders of witch belief; (2) that this was not paradoxical because their demonology was generated by their scientific commitments (Baconian empiricism required taking testimony to spirits seriously; anti-Hobbesian metaphysics required spirits to exist); and (3) that the standard narrative ('science defeated witchcraft') cannot account for Glanvill, since his demonology was a product of his science, not a residue from pre-scientific thinking. The Saducismus is therefore among the most important evidential texts for the revisionist interpretation of the relationship between the Scientific Revolution and witch prosecution.

key_arguments.concept: Sadducism (materialism) as the real epistemological error
key_arguments.claim: The rejection of witch-belief is not scientific scepticism but materialist dogmatism — the principled refusal to consider evidence for immaterial substance. The 'Sadducee' who denies spirits is more epistemologically dishonest than the witch-believer, because the empirical evidence for spirits (consistent testimony from reliable witnesses) meets the same standard as evidence for any other class of preternatural phenomena.

key_arguments.concept: Witch testimony as Baconian natural history
key_arguments.claim: The proper Royal Society method — collect testimony, cross-check against other testimony, identify consistent patterns, avoid premature theorization — applied to witch phenomena exactly as to any other preternatural event. Glanvill's case studies, including the Drummer of Tedworth investigation (conducted on-site), were natural history in the Baconian sense: evidence for the existence of immaterial substance collected by the same methods used for any other scientific inquiry.

key_arguments.concept: No spirit, no God (Henry More's addition)
key_arguments.claim: More's philosophical appendix made the theological stakes explicit: if Hobbesian materialism was correct and all apparent spirit-phenomena had mechanical explanations, the concept of an immaterial God became incoherent. The Saducismus was therefore simultaneously natural philosophy, demonology, and Anglican theology — all three domains required the same conclusion about the reality of spirits.

relation_to_database: Saducismus Triumphatus is the primary source for the glanvill-joseph-b1636 and more-henry-b1614 scholar entries. It is the key text cited in the natural-demonic-magic-distinction concept entry's discussion of how natural philosophy engaged with preternatural phenomena in the Restoration period. The work connects to the eschatological-witchcraft-postremus-furor concept entry through Cotton Mather's possible use of it at Salem.
scholarly_disagreement: The primary debate about Saducismus Triumphatus concerns the nature of Glanvill's scientific credentials and whether Clark overstates the integration of his demonological and scientific commitments. Simon Schaffer has argued there was 'no correlation between endorsement of the reality of spirits and support for witch trials' — figures like Boyle were interested in spirit evidence but did not advocate prosecution. John Webster's The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft (1677) was the most systematic contemporary refutation, attacking Glanvill's evidentiary standards. The influence of Saducismus Triumphatus on Cotton Mather and the Salem proceedings remains debated: circumstantial connections have been proposed but not securely documented. Barbara Shapiro and Michael Hunter have argued that Glanvill's witchcraft interests were more peripheral to his scientific identity than Clark suggests.
source_method: Published primary source: London, 1681 (posthumous, ed. Henry More); Stuart Clark, Thinking with Demons (1997/2001), Part II: Science, pp.356-375
